sections.h2: Selling a house in Lakewood, NJ
sections.html:
Lakewood is a flat, fast-growing township in Ocean County. However the house is sold, by agent, by owner or to a cash buyer, it passes through three desks: township code enforcement, the Ocean County Clerk's recording office and the state fee schedule.

Population reached 143,765 in the 2025 estimate, up from 135,158 in 2020, more than any other township in Ocean County. Households average 4.36 people, so bedroom count and floor plan weigh heavily with buyers. Owners live in 51.5% of the homes, and a typical owner-held house is valued at $466,700.

Median household income is $65,101 beside that $466,700 median home value, so many buyers lean on mortgages, family money or cash. That is one reason as-is offers are common on tired or oddly laid-out houses here.

Greenville, Seven Stars, South Lakewood and Lake Carasaljo are place names you will see on listings, and four man-made lakes (Carasaljo, Manetta, Shenandoah and Waddill) anchor several neighborhoods. If your house sits in the age-restricted Leisure Village or Leisure Village East, request that community's own resale rules in writing before you sign a contract.

Many families choose a home by walking distance to a yeshiva or school rather than by the public school zone, so ask your agent which side of a street a buyer would prefer. Buyers also ask about these links:

  • Garden State Parkway exit 89, which also feeds Route 70 after exit 88 closed permanently in November 2014.
  • Route 70, Route 88 and Route 9, plus county roads 526, 528, 547 and 549.
  • The Lakewood Bus Terminal, where NJ Transit routes 137 and 139 run toward New York's Port Authority, 317 toward Philadelphia, 67 toward Newark and 559 toward Atlantic City.

Start with the Township of Lakewood's Code Enforcement office at 212 4th Street, phone 732-364-3760. The rental and housing window is open 8:30 AM to 4 PM. A posted notice reminds owners of the smoke and carbon monoxide alarm requirement. Ask the staff what resale paperwork and inspection your closing date needs, and request the form list in writing.

The township's FAQ raises the question of a certificate of occupancy when selling a home, so get the current answer by phone. Ask about open permits too. Work done without a permit can cost up to $2,000 in penalties, plus $2,000 more for each additional week.

  • Permit review under the state construction code can take up to 20 business days.
  • The engineering section covers flood zone lookups, elevation certificates, property surveys and wetlands questions.
  • A rented house also needs a rental certificate of occupancy application on file ahead of a tenant change.

sections.h2: Who records a Lakewood deed, and what does the seller owe?
sections.html:
The Ocean County Clerk records Lakewood deeds. Its main office sits at 118 Washington Street in Toms River and answers at (732) 929-2018. Weekday hours run 8 to 4:30, and the counter stops taking filings at 4. The clerk also lists a Lakewood location at 225 4th Street, Room 211, phone (732) 370-8850.

At a median value of $466,700, a typical sale falls under the state realty transfer fee schedule for prices above $350,000. The seller pays that fee, and the rate climbs in steps as the price rises. Sales above $1 million add a graduated percentage fee of 1% to 3.5%, also charged to the seller.

Request a payoff figure from the township's tax collector before you list. The township holds an online sale each fall for delinquent taxes and water or sewer charges, so an account left unpaid may end up sold as a lien certificate against the house. A buyer's title company will find it either way, and it can hold up a closing for days. Settle the balance from the sale proceeds at closing, or pay it ahead of time so the title search comes back clean.

sections.h2: From offer to closing in Lakewood
sections.html:
The order of work is the same on every route. First, call Code Enforcement and ask what your closing date requires, so a certificate or alarm check does not surprise you in the last week. Second, pull the tax collector's payoff figure and any water or sewer balance. Third, gather the survey, permit records and leases. Fourth, sign a contract with written terms on who pays what. Fifth, close, and have the closing attorney or title agent send the deed to the Ocean County Clerk for recording.

A cash buyer skips the lender's appraisal and underwriting, which removes the steps most likely to delay a closing. It does not remove the township paperwork or the recording step, so the timeline still depends on how fast those desks respond. Tenants in place are workable: hand the buyer the lease and ask Code Enforcement about the rental certificate before the closing date is set.

When you compare offers, line up the price, the closing date, who orders any township certificate and who pays the state transfer fee. Two offers with the same headline number can leave you with different amounts at the table.

sections.h2: Which sale route suits a Lakewood house?
sections.html:
Choose by timeline and condition. A listing reaches the widest set of buyers, but it comes with showings, an appraisal and a township inspection step. Selling alone saves the commission and leaves the paperwork with you. A buyer paying cash as-is removes repairs and loan approval from the picture. Compare written terms, including who pays the transfer fee and who orders any township certificate.

Put the survey, permit records, current leases and latest tax bill in one folder before any offer arrives, and ask your title company for a copy of your recorded deed. Clean paperwork keeps Lakewood deals moving, while a late permit or occupancy question tends to stall them. At closing, the deed goes to the county clerk, the seller's fee is paid from proceeds, and any open tax balance is cleared.

faqs.q: Is a township inspection part of selling in Lakewood?
faqs.a: Ask the township. Code Enforcement at 732-364-3760 handles smoke and carbon monoxide alarm rules and resale paperwork, and its FAQ raises a certificate of occupancy question for home sellers. Get the requirement for your address before fixing a closing date.

faqs.q: Is the transfer fee my cost as a Lakewood seller?
faqs.a: Yes. The state bases it on the price in the deed and collects it when the Ocean County Clerk records the deed. Sales above $1 million also trigger a graduated percentage fee, again on the seller.

faqs.q: Which office records a Lakewood deed?
faqs.a: The Ocean County Clerk. The main office is in Toms River at (732) 929-2018, and a Lakewood location at 225 4th Street, Room 211 answers at (732) 370-8850.

faqs.q: What if my Lakewood house has open permits?
faqs.a: You can still sell, but deal with them first. Code Enforcement can tell you which permits are open, and unpermitted work can draw fines that grow weekly. A buyer or lender may require the permit closed before the sale.

faqs.q: Is cash faster than listing in Lakewood?
faqs.a: Often, because a cash sale skips mortgage approval and an appraisal. A listing may reach more buyers. Deed recording, the transfer fee and any township certificate apply either way, so compare the written terms.
